passage: Sudha, my girl, you were so quiet at dinner the first week in the new school, so I told you something I had never told you. I am Tanvir, your father. When I was nine, we moved towns, and I ate lunch alone for a month. I used to count the tiles in the corridor. You put your spoon down and said, "You did? Really?" Then you told me about the girl who laughed when you got the classroom wrong. After that we made a habit of Sunday walks to the river, just the two of us, and you talked more each time.

qa.q: How long did Tanvir eat lunch alone after his own move?
qa.a: He ate lunch alone for a month.

qa.q: What might Sudha have been feeling when she asked, "You did? Really?"
qa.a: She was probably relieved and surprised to learn her father had once felt as lost as she did, which made her feel less alone.

qa.q: What small step helped Sudha keep talking about school?
qa.a: The Sunday walks to the river with her father gave her a steady, relaxed time to share what happened during the week. 🙂

qa.q: Why might Tanvir have chosen to share his own story instead of just asking about her day?
qa.a: He may have thought that hearing his story would show her that feeling lost is normal and that she could talk to him without being judged.

grounding: A parent's own memory of feeling lost makes the child feel less alone, and a weekend outing becomes a settling routine.

passage: The first month after we moved to Nashik, I cried in the bathroom most nights so nobody would hear. I'm Vaibhav, and I thought I was the only person in the world who felt so lost. One night Papa knocked and sat on the edge of the tub. He told me that when he was nine, his family moved from a village to Pune, and he hid under the stairs at his new school for a whole week. 'I thought everyone could tell I didn't belong,' he said. I stared at him. Papa, who talks to everyone? After that, every Sunday he took me and my little sister Hafsa to the Godavari ghats for vada pav. It became our thing. Slowly, Nashik started to feel like somewhere I lived, not just somewhere I was.

qa.q: Where did Papa hide at his new school?
qa.a: Under the stairs, for a whole week.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel on hearing Papa's story?
qa.a: Surprised and much less alone; Vaibhav had thought nobody else ever felt so lost 🙂

qa.q: What small routine helped settle Vaibhav?
qa.a: Sunday trips to the Godavari ghats for vada pav with Papa and Hafsa.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt seeing Vaibhav so lost?
qa.a: Worried and protective, and reminded of his own lonely week, which is why he chose to share it.

grounding: A child who feels lost after a move hears that the father once felt the same, feels less alone, and settles through a weekly outing.

passage:
Counsellor's note, by Bhavna Kulkarni, school counselling room.
Ramesh, Class 4, new this term, came in with his father after two weeks of eating lunch alone and saying little. Ramesh sat with his arms folded. His father spoke first. 'When we moved to Delhi, I was younger than you. I didn't speak Hindi well. I felt lost for a whole year.' Ramesh looked up for the first time. 'A whole year?' 'Nearly. It got better when my mother started taking me to the Sunday market.' Ramesh's arms uncrossed. He admitted that he misses his old cricket ground most. We agreed on a small plan: a Saturday outing with his father to find a new ground. I will check in with Ramesh next Friday.

qa.q: What did Ramesh's arms uncrossing suggest?
qa.a: He felt less alone and more open after hearing that his father had also felt lost.

qa.q: What plan did they agree on?
qa.a: A Saturday outing with his father to find a new cricket ground, with a check-in next Friday.

qa.q: How might the father feel sharing his own lost year?
qa.a: A little exposed but hopeful, wanting Ramesh to know the feeling can pass.

grounding: A counsellor's note records a new boy opening up after his father shares that he too felt lost in a new place.
